transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

I’ve started going out of my way to avoid any job that involves getting up high, and when I can’t avoid it, I’m barely able to stay up there long enough to do my work. It's getting to the point where it's really affecting my reputation on the job site, and I need to figure out how to handle it.
When you are high up, do you feel intense fear or panic specifically about the height itself, even if you know you are physically safe?

Yes, absolutely. Even when I know the structure is solid and I'm clipped in with safety gear, my chest tightens up and my heart starts pounding like crazy. My legs go completely rubbery and my mind just jumps straight to pictures of me tipping over the edge.
Do you have this same intense fear or avoidance with other specific things, like flying, needles, animals, or enclosed spaces, or is it mainly only when you are up high?

No, it's really just heights that get to me. I don't have any issues with needles, animals, or being in tight spaces at all. It is strictly being up high that triggers this panic and makes me want to run.
Has this fear of heights been present for at least 6 months, and has it been causing significant problems in your work or daily life?

Yes, it's been going on for a little over a year now, ever since a scaffolding accident on one of my job sites. It's causing real problems at work with my supervisors questioning my reliability because I'm avoiding high site walks, and it's even spilling into my personal life with volunteer fire trainings and trips with my buddies.
Since the scaffolding accident, do you also have unwanted memories, nightmares, or feel on edge when you’re reminded of the accident itself, even when you’re not up high?

No, I don't get nightmares or flashbacks about the accident, and I'm not tense when I'm on the ground. My panic is strictly triggered by actually being up high or knowing I have to go up. As long as my feet are on solid ground, I feel completely fine.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has a persistent, marked, and situation-specific fear of heights with immediate panic symptoms, avoidance, and clear functional impairment at work and in daily activities, present for over 1 year. The fear is confined to heights and is not better explained by PTSD, as he denies re-experiencing, nightmares, hypervigilance, or ground-level trauma reminders.
